bridge: N06 introduced HTTP and proxies; N04 introduced message framing. Use only supplied traces or the dedicated isolated lab.
teaching:
### Remember why framing is needed

A connection can carry more than one request. Each receiving component needs rules for the request line, headers and body length. That is framing: identifying the boundaries of one message.

### Compare the two interpretations

A front proxy may forward bytes using one interpretation while the backend parses them using another. If they disagree about a body boundary, leftover bytes can be treated as part of a later request. This family of issues is called request smuggling.

The vulnerability depends on the actual chain of parsers and protocol conversions. Seeing an unusual header alone does not prove the disagreement exists.

### Remove ambiguity

Use consistent maintained components and reject invalid or ambiguous message forms under the deployed protocol rules. Pay attention to conversion between HTTP versions and to any intermediary that rewrites headers.

### Inspect without overclaiming

For a supplied trace, mark what each parser believes the request length to be. State the observed response, the connection reuse assumptions and any missing backend evidence. In a shared live system, such experiments can affect other users, which is why this course confines them to isolated authorised targets.
example:
Abstract fixture: byte positions 0..19
Front parser assumes body ends after position 9.
Back parser assumes body ends after position 14.
Bytes 10..14 are therefore interpreted differently.

Parser F: request 1=[0..9], next begins 10
Parser B: request 1=[0..14], next begins 15
Question: can both sides safely reuse this connection as if aligned?
explanation: Positions are inclusive: 0..9 contains 10 bytes, while 0..14 contains 15. Parser F leaves position 10 as the next request’s start; parser B treats 10..14 as part of the first request and starts the next at 15. Thus the same five bytes have conflicting meanings. The model is not valid HTTP syntax. A status code alone does not establish this parser path.
exercise: Draw both boundary views for the supplied 20-byte fixture. Then use matching end positions 9/9 and explain the difference. State two requirements for a defensive proxy/backend configuration review.
solution: Draw F as [0..9] | [10..19] and B as [0..14] | [15..19]. In the 9/9 variant both start the next request at 10, so this particular boundary disagreement is absent. That does not prove the requests or implementation are otherwise safe. Review strict framing validation, consistent interpretation through each proxy/translation hop, and how ambiguous messages are rejected and connections closed rather than reused out of alignment.
challenge: Write a provider-lab evidence plan identifying scope, front/back protocol assumptions, baseline, one controlled variation, expected boundary effect and a safe stop condition. Explain why success against one parser version does not prove all deployments share the fault.
challenge_solution: Parsing and translation behaviour depend on actual components/configuration. Evidence must support the tested chain and avoid extrapolation. Do not send framing experiments to unrelated production sites.
